'''''Ulva linza''''' is a [[green alga]] in the family [[Ulvaceae]] that can be found in [[British Isles]].<ref name=marlin>{{cite web|url= http://www.marlin.ac.uk/speciesinformation.php?speciesID=4542|title=A green seaweed - Ulva linza|accessdate=March 23, 2013}}</ref>

==Description==
''Ulva (Enteromorpha) linza (Linnaeus)<ref name="LM Granhag 2004">LM Granhag, JA Finlay, PR Jonsson, JA Callow & ME Callow (2004) Roughness-dependent Removal of Settled Spores of the Green Alga Ulva (syn. Enteromorpha) Exposed to Hydrodynamic Forces from a Water Jet, Biofouling, 20:2, 117-122, DOI: 10.1080/08927010410001715482</ref>'' is a {{convert|30|cm}} (sometimes {{convert|45|cm}})<ref name=seaweedindustry>{{cite web|url=https://seaweedindustry.com/seaweed/type/ulva-linza|title=Ulva linza|publisher=Sea Weed Industry|accessdate=March 23, 2013|archive-date=March 31, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140331232631/https://seaweedindustry.com/seaweed/type/ulva-linza|url-status=live}}</ref> long green alga that grows in bright green clusters of tubes or flat strips. It has unbranched thalli that often have a frilled margin.  The [[thallus]] middle is greater than its base and can be as wide as {{convert|5|cm}}.<ref name=marlin/> Its ruffled blades are {{convert|1|-|4|cm}} long while its cells are {{convert|10|-|15|μm}} in diameter.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.seaweedsofalaska.com/species.asp?SeaweedID=14|title=Green String Lettuce|publisher=Seaweeds of Alaska|accessdate=March 23, 2013|archive-date=August 1, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120801224606/http://www.seaweedsofalaska.com/species.asp?SeaweedID=14|url-status=live}}</ref>

''Ulva linza'' found in Rhode Island have branched or unbranched flattened tubes.<ref name="Guidone, M. 2013">Guidone, M., Thornber, C., Wysor, B., & O'Kelly, C. J. (2013). Molecular and morphological diversity of narragansett bay (RI, USA) ulva (ulvales, chlorophyta) populations. Journal of Phycology, 49(5), 979-995. doi:10.1111/jpy.12108</ref>  The thallus length ranges from 1.9 –36 cm with a mean length of 18.6 cm.  The thallus width ranges from 0.2 to 4.8 cm with a mean width of 1.4 cm.<ref name="Guidone, M. 2013"/>  ''Ulva linza'' can be distinguished by its smooth thallus, most with a ruffled margin.<ref name="Guidone, M. 2013"/>  Ulva linza can tolerate a wide range of salinities and water qualities.<ref name="Callow, M. E. 1997">Callow, M. E., Callow, J. A., Pickett-Heaps, J. D., & Wetherbee, R. (1997). Primary adhesion of enteromorpha (chlorophyta, ulvales) propagules: Quantitative settlement studies and video microscopy. Journal of Phycology, 33(6), 938-947. doi:10.1111/j.0022-3646.1997.00938.x</ref>  Laboratory experiments have shown a broad tolerance to the environmental conditions of irradiance, temperature, salinity, and a wide range of nitrogen and phosphorus concentrations.<ref>Taylor, R., Fletcher, R. L., & Raven, J. A. (2001). Preliminary studies on the growth of selected 'green tide' algae in laboratory culture: Effects of irradiance, temperature, salinity and nutrients on growth rate.Botanica Marina, 44(4), 327-336. doi:10.1515/BOT.2001.042</ref>

[[File:Ulva linza.jpg|thumb|Photo of Ulva linza in Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island. Photo by Kayla Kurtz.]]

[[File:Ulva linza harvested in Spring 2019.jpg|thumb|Photo of Ulva linza harvested from Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island. Photo by Kayla Kurtz.]]

''Ulva linza'' alternates between sexual (gametophyte producing gametes) and asexual (sporophyte producing zoospores) stages.  Spores with two or four flagella are released from the thalli. Zoospores with four flagella (quadriflagellated zoospores) rapidly settle on surfaces.  Biflagellate spores are typed as female (+) gametes, male (-) gametes, or asexual biflagellate zoospores.<ref name="Callow, M. E. 1997"/>

''Ulva'' species have been reported as a dominant species leading to blooms of green macroalgae often referred to as “green tides.”  These green tides and marine fouling are attributed to their thallus morphological characteristics, fast growth rates in eutrophic ecosystems, and rapid uptake and assimilation of nutrients.<ref name="Luo, M. B. 2012">Luo, M. B., Liu, F., & Xu, Z. L. (2012). Growth and nutrient uptake capacity of two co-occurring species, ulva prolifera and ulva linza. Aquatic Botany, 100, 18-24. doi:10.1016/j.aquabot.2012.03.006</ref>  These blooms are generally explained by eutrophication caused by increased nutrient loads (i.e., nitrogen and phosphorus) from events such as runoff, sewage outflow, and upwelling.<ref name="Luo, M. B. 2012"/>

==Habitat==
They are littoral and [[sublittoral]] species which grow in muddy estuaries attached to pebbles or docks. They also can be found on [[rock (geology)|rocks]] or in [[rock pool]]s.<ref name=marlin/>  Ulva linza can be found in the upper intertidal zone of seashores.<ref name="Finlay, J. A. 2002">Finlay, J. A., Callow, M. E., Schultz, M. P., Swain, G. W., & Callow, J. A. (2002). Adhesion strength of settled spores of the green alga enteromorpha. Biofouling, 18(4), 251-256. doi:10.1080/08927010290029010</ref>

Ulva linza has been found in Wembury beach, UK,<ref name="LM Granhag 2004"/> Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island,<ref name="Guidone, M. 2013"/> the British Isles,<ref name="Guidone, M. 2013"/> and China.<ref name="Guidone, M. 2013"/>

==Uses==
The species is edible and therefore can be used as food and in cosmetic products.<ref name=seaweedindustry/>  Ulva linza is used as a model organism for biofouling in marine environments.<ref name="Finlay, J. A. 2002"/>  It has been found on a variety of man-made structures including ships’ hulls.<ref>6.	Finlay, J. A., Callow, M. E., Schultz, M. P., Swain, G. W., & Callow, J. A. (2002). Adhesion strength of settled spores of the green alga enteromorpha. Biofouling, 18(4), 251-256. doi:10.1080/08927010290029010</ref>
